title: Second Day Morning: God Over All

sections.heading: Seeing you as the God over everything
sections.text:
Father, you are enough in yourself, and everything else depends on you. You made all things, and you keep them going by your powerful word. The parts of your ways we cannot see are still under your rule. The wind, the clouds, the nations, the passing years, and the whole world are not outside your command.

We are brief. One generation comes after another, and our bodies return to dust. Even the heavens and the earth we know will not last forever. But you do not wear out, change, decay, or come to an end. You are God over all, blessed forever. We worship you as infinitely great and glorious.
theological_themes: God is self-sufficient, creator, sustainer, and ruler over all creation.
Human life and the present creation are temporary; God alone is eternal and unchanging.
Worship begins with seeing the difference between God’s permanence and our dependence.

scripture_references.connection: This passage speaks of the Son sustaining all things by his powerful word, grounding the prayer’s confession that creation continues only because God upholds it.

The psalm contrasts the heavens and earth, which will wear out, with God, who remains the same forever. That directly supports the prayer’s movement from human and cosmic transience to God’s unchanging life.

sections.heading: Remembering that we live because you care for us
sections.text:
And yet, great as you are, you have not treated us as too small to notice. We come from you, and we are under your care. Your hands made us and shaped us. You have watched over us with a love deeper than even the best love of a father or mother.

You have kept us alive. You have held us when we could have fallen. We are here this morning because you have guarded our lives and carried us through more dangers than we know.
theological_themes: The transcendent God is also personally near to his creatures.
God’s care is tender, faithful, and more dependable than human parental love.
Our continued life is not self-generated but preserved by God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the God who made the world gives life and breath to all people, and that in him we live and move and have our being. This supports the prayer’s confession that we are God’s creatures and depend on his care for every moment.
The psalm praises God for keeping his people among the living and not letting their feet slip. That closely matches the prayer’s gratitude for God preserving life and stability.

sections.heading: Thanking you for mercy we must not forget
sections.text:
You have given us what we need for life with you. So help us bless you at all times and not forget your kindness.

You have forgiven our sins. You have cared for our bodies and souls. You have rescued our lives from ruin. You have surrounded us with steadfast love and mercy. You have filled our mouths with good things. You have renewed our strength when we were worn down.

Keep us from taking these mercies for granted. Make us a thankful people who remember what we have received from your hand.
theological_themes: God provides everything necessary for life and godliness.
God’s mercy includes forgiveness, rescue, sustaining care, provision, and renewal.
Thanksgiving is a faithful response to remembered grace.

scripture_references.connection: Peter says God’s divine power has granted believers all things that pertain to life and godliness. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that what we need for faithful life with God comes from him.

This psalm calls God’s people not to forget his benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, steadfast love, provision, and renewal. The prayer intentionally gathers these same mercies into thanksgiving.

sections.heading: Asking your Word to shape our whole life
sections.text:
Let your Scriptures rule us in every part of life. Teach us what to believe, correct us where we are wrong, train us in what is good, and guide us in the ordinary duties you have given us.

May the way we live make your truth look beautiful, not only in worship but in our work, our homes, our speech, our responsibilities, and our care for one another. Let our lives fit the gospel we confess. Amen.
theological_themes: Scripture is God’s authority for belief, correction, training, and faithful living.
God’s people are called to live ordinary duties in a way that commends his doctrine.
Faith is meant to be visible in the whole pattern of life, not confined to formal worship.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Scripture is breathed out by God and equips God’s people for every good work. This directly supports asking that Scripture govern every part of life and duty.

Paul urges believers to live faithfully in ordinary responsibilities so that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. This explains the prayer’s request that our conduct make God’s teaching visible and honorable.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about the heavens vanishing and the earth dissolving was rendered as the temporary nature of the present creation without trying to specify an end-times timetable.
The phrase about God healing diseases echoes Psalm 103. It was rendered as God’s merciful care for bodies and souls, not as a promise that every illness will be immediately healed in this life.
The original says we are God’s offspring and care. This was kept as creaturely dependence on God, not expanded into the distinct doctrine of saving adoption.
significant_interpretive_choices: The images of darkness, wind, clouds, and nations were summarized as signs of God’s rule over both visible and hidden realities, rather than reproduced one by one in archaic poetic form.

The phrase 'more than parental love, more than maternal tenderness' was expressed as love deeper than the best human fatherly or motherly love, preserving the force without implying any deficiency in God’s fatherhood.
The phrase 'adorn thy doctrine' was interpreted in line with Titus 2 as living in a way that commends the gospel and God’s teaching in ordinary responsibilities.
